title: The use of Horizon graphs to visualize bilateral biomechanical time-series of multiple joints
author: Okai-Nobrega, Santos, et al.
materials: RoMpp = Peak to peak range of motion

Despite the benefits offered by HG, some limitations must be indicated. The analysis is limited to a few cycles (e.g., five cycles) since plotting several cycles could be challenging and difficult to visualize. Also, processing and full implementation of the method may not be straightforward [19]. Fortunately, online tools and programming codes for implementing the method are freely available to users [20]. Furthermore, we added the algorithm implemented in R as Supplementary Material to help researchers interested in the method.

steps.title: Recruit participants and obtain consent
steps.instruction: Select two adult runners: (1) non‑injured (age 28 yr, height 1.61 m, mass 56.1 kg) and (2) injured (age 29 yr, height 1.63 m, mass 71.9 kg, history of right shank stress fracture). Have each sign the informed‑consent form approved by the university ethical committee (ETIC 0526.0.203.000‑10).

steps.title: Configure treadmill and motion capture system
steps.instruction: Set a treadmill to the participant’s self‑selected running speed. Install three CODA position‑scanner units (CODA system, Charnwood Dynamics, Leicestershire, England) and record at 100 Hz.

steps.title: Record sagittal joint angular displacements
steps.instruction: Capture the angular displacement of the hip, knee and ankle joints in the sagittal plane while the participant runs. Process the raw marker data with Visual 3D (C‑Motion Inc., Germantown, MD, USA) using a standard rigid‑body model. Define positive values as hip/knee flexion and ankle dorsiflexion; negative values as hip/knee extension and ankle plantar‑flexion.

steps.title: Calculate symmetry ratio time series
steps.instruction: For each time point compute SR = (R − L) / RoMpp, where R = right joint angle, L = left joint angle, and RoMpp = peak‑to‑peak range of motion for that joint. Use RoMpp to avoid artificial inflation when the denominator is small.

steps.title: Normalize each gait cycle to 101 points
steps.instruction: Identify individual running cycles (stance to swing). Resample each cycle so that it contains exactly 101 equally spaced data points (baseline set to 0° for all series). When displaying multiple cycles, concatenate the normalized cycles (e.g., two cycles → 202 points; five cycles → 505 points).

steps.title: Generate horizon graph using R algorithm
steps.instruction: Run the provided R script (Supplementary Material) to create a horizon graph for each joint:

substeps.instruction: Segment each normalized line chart into uniformly sized, non‑overlapping bands (three bands, giving a height reduction factor of three).
Reflect negative‑value portions around the zero‑degree baseline.
Assign colors: positive bands → blue; negative bands → red/yellow. Color intensity encodes band level (magnitude).
Layer the three bands for each series (right joint, left joint, SR) so that the SR appears as the third layer.
Add vertical dotted lines to separate cycles and label axes (left axis = joint angles, right axis = band magnitude).

steps.title: Identify MAX, SIMI, and DISC features
steps.instruction: From the horizon graph extract: (i) MAX – the peak values of each joint’s time series; (ii) SIMI – symmetry information from the SR layer (blue = right‑side dominance, red = left‑side dominance, intensity = asymmetry level); (iii) DISC – visual relationships of peak timing among hip, knee and ankle across cycles.
